newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. Stealths return to Gulf War battleground.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Stealths return to Gulf War battleground.

text.p: Eight U.S. Stealth bombers at the centre of fresh confrontation between Kuwait and Iraq flew into Kuwait on Friday on a mission that U.S. officials have said may involve action against Kuwait's former occupier.

A military source said by telephone the black jets, returning to the 1991 Gulf War battleground where they won prominence with radar evading capability, arrived in the early evening after a 20-hour, non-stop flight from Holloman Air Force base in New Mexico in the United States.
There were no further details. U.S. military and other officials were unable immediately to confirm the arrival of the planes.

Iraq, in a fresh standoff with Washington over the expansion of a southern no-fly zone, told Kuwait on Thursday it would be committing an act of war if it allowed U.S. Stealth warplanes to use its territory for attacks on his country.
The U.S. jets were moving into position for possible raids against Iraq after Iraqi forces fired a surface-to-air missile at U.S. fighters over northern Iraq on Wednesday.
Military analysts expect the eight bombers to be based at Ahmad al-Jaber air base southwest of Kuwait City, the more southerly of Kuwait's two main military airfields.

They explain that Ahmad al-Jaber is a more secure base because it is further away from the Iraqi border and has more sophisticated maintenance equipment and personnel than at Ali al-Salem base -- a high priority even though Stealth maintenance crews have already arrived in Kuwait.

Stealths flew 1,271 combat missions in the six-week Gulf War, one third of them over Baghdad, scoring an 80 to 85 percent hit rate, compared to a less than 40 percent hit rate from other bombers flown in the conflict, Pentagon figures show.
During the war the Stealths dropped mostly 900 kg (2,000 lb) GBU27 Paveway laser-guided bombs on missions that lasted an average 5-1/2 hours.
The aircraft caused terror in Iraq because they proved to be the best aircraft at delivering "smart" munitions through windows and ventilation shafts.
The aircraft have a crew of one and are difficult to detect by radar because they are coated in radar absorbable material made of aluminium and various composite materials.
"It was an expensive bird to develop but it doesn't miss," a U.S. military analyst said. "We don't want to lose anybody."
